newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists fail in bid to hand letter to caucus.
newsitem.headline: HK activists fail in bid to hand letter to caucus.

text.p: Democracy activists on Saturday tried to submit a grievance letter to a Beijing-appointed caucus overseeing Hong Kong's mid-1997 return to China but were barred from entering its local premises.

About 30 protesters sought to hand the letter to the local office of the Preparatory Committee (PC) to air their opposition to some Chinese policies on Hong Kong, including the formation of the Selection Committee (SC) whose members were to be named in Beijing on Saturday.

Chanting slogans and brandishing banners, they marched through Hong Kong's crowded streets to a building where the PC office is located on the 15th floor but found about 40 police blocking the elevator lobby.
A police spokeswoman told Reuters the police were deployed only for "calm management" and did not bar the protesters from entering the PC office.
The building's security force told protesters they could not enter the office, she added.
"The building's management said the Preparatory Committee did not allow us to go up to its office," said Andrew Cheng, a legislator and one of the protestors.
Relevant PC officials were not available for comment.
A man claiming to be a staff member from the PC office asked the demonstrators to give him the letter.
But disgruntled activists instead tore it up in front of him.
"We represent Hong Kong people. The Preparatory Commitee should reflect Hong Kong people's views (to Beijing). Why can't we go up (to its office)?" Cheng said.

"We are not at all surprised that they said they wouldn't let us in the Preparatory Committee's secretariat office because the Chinese government has given Hong Kong people and overseas societies a clear impression that they are definitely not interested in listeing to dissenting views."" said lawmaker Emily Lau, who was among the protesters.

The letter said the formation of the Selection Committee, which will pick Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader and appoint a provisional legislature in place of the elected Legislative Council following the handover, was not democratic.
It also said establshment of the provisional legislature was not democratic and lacked legal basis, and accused China of stemming peaceful petitions.

On Friday Hong Kong democracy advocates Wong Chung-ki and Chui Pak-tai were ordered out of China. The previous day two others, Andrew To and Chan Kwok-leung, were barred from crossing over the Chinese border.
The four activists had planned to petition the PC during its meeting in Beijing on arrangements for the handover.
